items.subject: Chemistry
items.body: Experiment 1: Action of dilute HCl on Sodium Carbonate (Na₂CO₃) and Sodium Hydrogen Carbonate (NaHCO₃).

metadata.aim: To study the reaction of dilute hydrochloric acid on sodium carbonate and sodium hydrogen carbonate and test the gas evolved.
procedure: Take about 0.5g of Na₂CO₃ in test tube A and 0.5g of NaHCO₃ in test tube B.
Add 2 mL of dilute HCl to both test tubes.
Observe brisk effervescence due to carbon dioxide gas evolution.
Pass the evolved gas through freshly prepared lime water.
Notice lime water turning milky due to insoluble calcium carbonate formation.
Pass excess CO₂ gas and observe the solution becoming clear again as soluble calcium bicarbonate forms.
metadata.result: Dilute acids react with metal carbonates and hydrogen carbonates to liberate Carbon Dioxide gas (CO₂), which turns lime water milky.
precautions: Always handle dilute HCl with care using a dropper.
Ensure lime water is freshly prepared for accurate milkiness observation.
Do not inhale the gas directly from the mouth of the test tube.

items.subject: Chemistry
items.body: Experiment 2: Finding the pH of given samples using pH paper / universal indicator.

metadata.aim: To determine the pH of given samples (Dilute HCl, NaOH solution, Ethanoic acid, Lemon juice, Water, NaHCO₃ solution) using pH paper.
procedure: Place clean watch glasses on a clean laboratory table.
Put a strip of pH paper on each watch glass.
Using a clean glass rod, place a drop of each sample solution on separate pH paper strips.
Observe the color produced on the pH paper instantly.
Match the observed color with the standard pH color chart provided on the box.
Record the corresponding numerical pH value and classify the sample as acidic, neutral, or basic.
metadata.result: pH values < 7 indicate acidic nature, pH = 7 indicates neutral, and pH > 7 indicates basic nature.
precautions: Wash the glass rod thoroughly with distilled water before testing a new solution.
Compare the color of pH paper while it is still moist.
Keep pH paper strips away from acid/base vapors in the laboratory.

items.subject: Chemistry
items.body: Experiment 3: Properties of Acids & Bases (HCl & NaOH) by reaction with Litmus, Zinc metal, and Na₂CO₃.

metadata.aim: To study the properties of acids (HCl) and bases (NaOH) by their reactions with Blue/Red litmus, Zinc metal, and Sodium Carbonate.
procedure: Test 2 mL of HCl and NaOH separately with Red and Blue litmus papers.
Add zinc granules to 2 mL of dilute HCl in a test tube. Observe gas evolution.
Bring a burning matchstick near the mouth of the test tube to test for Hydrogen (pop sound).
Add zinc granules to 2 mL of dilute NaOH and warm gently over a flame.
Test the gas evolved from NaOH + Zn with a burning matchstick.
Add Na₂CO₃ to both solutions and check for CO₂ evolution.
metadata.result: Acids turn blue litmus red and react with carbonates to yield CO₂. Both acids and strong bases react with active metals like Zinc to liberate H₂ gas.
precautions: Warm the NaOH and Zinc mixture gently; avoid boiling vigorously.
Hold the burning matchstick at a safe distance from the tube mouth when testing H₂.

items.subject: Chemistry
items.body: Experiment 4: Performing and observing four basic types of chemical reactions.

metadata.aim: To perform and observe the four types of chemical reactions: Combination, Decomposition, Displacement, and Double Displacement.
procedure: Combination: Add water to quicklime (CaO) in a beaker. Feel the container become very hot (exothermic).
Decomposition: Heat green FeSO₄ crystals in a dry boiling tube. Observe color change from green to brown (Fe₂O₃) and smell choking SO₂/SO₃ gas.
Displacement: Dip clean iron nails into blue CuSO₄ solution. Observe blue color fading to light green (FeSO₄) and brown Cu coating on nail.
Double Displacement: Mix Na₂SO₄ solution with BaCl₂ solution. Observe immediate white precipitate formation of BaSO₄.

defaultRows.observations: Blue solution turns green, brown deposit

metadata.result: Chemical reactions are classified based on bond rearrangement into combination, decomposition, single displacement, and double displacement precipitate reactions.
precautions: Never point the mouth of the heating tube towards yourself or neighbors while heating FeSO₄.
Clean iron nails with sandpaper before dipping into copper sulphate solution.

items.subject: Chemistry
items.body: Experiment 5: Action of Zn, Fe, Cu, Al metals on salt solutions (ZnSO₄, FeSO₄, CuSO₄, Al₂(SO₄)₃).

metadata.aim: To observe the action of Zn, Fe, Cu, and Al metals on aqueous salt solutions of ZnSO₄, FeSO₄, CuSO₄, and Al₂(SO₄)₃ and arrange them in decreasing order of reactivity.
procedure: Take four test tubes containing solutions of ZnSO₄, FeSO₄, CuSO₄, and Al₂(SO₄)₃ respectively.
Dip cleaned Zinc strips into all four tubes and note displacement reactions after 20 minutes.
Repeat the experiment using Iron nails, Copper strips, and Aluminium strips.
Record which metals displace other metals from their salt solutions.
Deduce relative reactivity: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal.
metadata.result: The decreasing order of metal reactivity is: Aluminium (Al) > Zinc (Zn) > Iron (Fe) > Copper (Cu).
precautions: Clean metal strips with sandpaper to remove oxide film before dipping.
Allow at least 15-20 minutes for displacement reactions to show clear color changes.

items.subject: Physics
items.body: Experiment 6: Studying the dependence of potential difference (V) on current (I) across a resistor and determining its resistance.

metadata.aim: To study the dependence of potential difference (V) across a resistor on the current (I) passing through it and determine its resistance by plotting a V-I graph.
procedure: Connect battery, key, ammeter, unknown resistor, and rheostat in series.
Connect voltmeter in parallel across the unknown resistor.
Check zero error in ammeter and voltmeter before starting.
Insert key and adjust rheostat to get minimum current reading on ammeter.
Record ammeter reading (I) and voltmeter reading (V).
Shift rheostat slider to 5 different positions, recording V and I at each step.
Calculate R = V/I for each trial and plot V vs I on a linear graph.
metadata.result: The ratio V/I is constant, confirming Ohm's Law. The mean resistance of the resistor is R = 4.99 Ω.
precautions: Always connect ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel.
Remove plug key between observations to prevent resistance wire heating.
Clean connecting wire ends with sandpaper to lower contact resistance.

items.subject: Physics
items.body: Experiment 7: Determination of equivalent resistance of two resistors in series and parallel combinations.

metadata.aim: To determine the equivalent resistance of two given resistors when connected in series and parallel combinations.
procedure: Connect resistors R₁ and R₂ end-to-end in series with ammeter and battery.
Measure potential difference V across series combination and current I. Compute R_s = V/I.
Compare measured R_s with theoretical value (R₁ + R₂).
Connect R₁ and R₂ across two common points in parallel combination.
Measure total current I and potential difference V across parallel setup. Compute R_p = V/I.
Compare measured R_p with theoretical value (R₁R₂ / (R₁ + R₂)).
metadata.result: Series equivalent resistance R_s = R₁ + R₂ (15 Ω). Parallel equivalent resistance R_p = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂) (3.33 Ω). Theoretical values match experimental results.
precautions: Ensure tight connections at all terminals to avoid artificial contact resistance.
Verify ammeter polarities (+ to positive battery terminal) before closing key.

items.subject: Biology
items.body: Experiment 8: Preparing a temporary mount of a leaf peel to show stomata under a microscope.

metadata.aim: To prepare a temporary stained mount of a leaf peel (Rheo or Tradescantia) to observe stomata under a compound microscope.
procedure: Pluck a fresh leaf of Rheo or Tradescantia and tear it obliquely to peel off a thin epidermal layer from lower surface.
Place the transparent leaf peel in a watch glass containing distilled water.
Add 2-3 drops of Safranine stain to the watch glass and leave for 2 minutes.
Wash excess stain from peel with clean distilled water.
Transfer stained peel to center of a clean glass slide using forceps.
Add a drop of glycerine over the peel and cover gently with coverslip using a needle to avoid air bubbles.
Observe under low power (10x) and high power (40x) objectives of microscope.

defaultRows.function: Regulates opening and closing of pore
Provides water/turgor support to guard cells

metadata.result: Stomata are present on lower epidermis of leaves, each consisting of a microscopic pore guarded by two kidney-shaped guard cells containing chloroplasts.
precautions: Always take the peel from the lower epidermal surface where stomata density is highest.
Avoid air bubbles under the coverslip by lowering it gently with a mounted needle.
